proposals.name: Spoken in-character line versus third-person description of the type
proposals.instruction: Score how far the tweet is a line UTTERED BY the person/world the hashtag evokes, rather than an outside observer's description OF that person/world. 10 = the whole text is direct speech or first-person report that only that character would say, with no framing ('Y'all watch this'; 'That's my uncledad!'; 'Tell you what.'; 'Married My Truck'). 5 = mixed, e.g. first-person but stated as a fact about oneself rather than performed. 0 = a clinical third-person label or field note about the type, with no speaker inside it ('multiple COPS appearances'; 'possum casserole night'; 'Family reunion Rohypnol'). Judge only voice/deixis, not how funny or offensive the content is.
proposals.rationale: The strongest single split in the slice. R10, R22, R44, R20, R37 are all performed utterances the dense side favours; R04, R11, R51, R26, R47 cover comparable subject matter but are written as anthropological captions. A scorecard built from content properties scores both alike because the TOPIC is identical; only the enunciation differs, so performance is exactly the property the card cannot see.

proposals.name: Punchline-first delivery with tags trailing behind
proposals.instruction: Score the ORDER in which the reader meets the joke. 10 = the first characters of the tweet are the joke itself; handles and hashtags come after it, so the payload lands before any metadata ('Solar? My NECK! #RedneckIn3Words @midnight'). 5 = joke is split across or interrupted by tags. 0 = the reader must pass through '@handle' plus the hashtag (and any other boilerplate) before reaching a single word of joke ('@midnight #GOPMovies Kill Bill of Rights'). Score placement only; do not re-judge the joke.
proposals.rationale: Near-total surface separation in this slice: R03, R37, R42, R33, R49 lead with the line, while R08, R27, R57, R31, R34 lead with '@midnight' plus hashtag. Beyond raw ordering this indexes composition posture (writing a line versus filling a reply box), which a content-only scorecard has no slot for.

proposals.name: Well-formed utterance versus bare noun-pile filling the word count
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry is a syntactically complete unit of language or a stack of juxtaposed nouns that merely reaches the required word count. 10 = a grammatical clause or idiomatic phrase with a verb, an imperative, or a genuine predication ('Married My Truck'; 'But we're we really?'; 'Dog: My Copilot'). 5 = an elliptical but idiomatic noun phrase that reads as natural English ('Road kill buffet'). 0 = two or three unconnected nouns concatenated with no syntax and no idiom, readable only as a keyword list ('raccoon penis toothpick'; 'Rodeo Baby Conception'). Do not reward or penalise topic.
proposals.rationale: R47, R11, R26, R05 hit the count by stacking nouns; R37, R45, R46, R10 hit the same count with real syntax. A scorecard that checks 'meets the N-word constraint' and 'names something on-theme' scores the noun piles full marks, because it counts words and topical hits rather than asking whether the words form an utterance a person could say.

proposals.name: Implies an off-screen scene with a before and after
proposals.instruction: Score how much unstated story the line forces the reader to construct. 10 = a short line that unmistakably implies events preceding and following it, so the reader involuntarily pictures the whole scene ('Y'all watch this'; 'Mother visits me, stays FOREVER'; 'Forgot Sunscreen Silly'). 5 = a situation is evoked but static, with no implied consequence. 0 = a static attribute, ingredient list, or label with no temporal extent at all ('Corn syrup and salt'). Judge implied narrative, not explicit narration; explicitly narrating the whole event should score LOW on this criterion, not high.
proposals.rationale: R10 and R09 are famous-last-words setups whose entire payload is the unwritten consequence; R38 and R54 both hinge on a duration word that opens a future. Compare R16 and R05, which state a content noun and stop. Scorecards reward what is present in the text; this criterion targets what is deliberately absent, which is why it is invisible to a bank of positive content checks.

proposals.name: Deadpan literal accuracy used instead of joke scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score entries that carry no visible joke machinery (no pun, no substitution, no exaggeration) and land purely because the flat statement is uncomfortably or affectionately true of the target. 10 = a plain, sincere-sounding assertion with zero comic construction that is nonetheless a precise portrait ('The 4th of July'; 'God Bless Texas!'; 'Bacon goes in everything'). 5 = mostly plain but with a mild comic tilt. 0 = an obviously engineered gag whose humour is entirely in the device, or a plain statement that is simply inaccurate/inert about the target. A judge should ask: with no joke apparatus at all, does the flat truth still hit?
proposals.rationale: R06, R07, R56 contain no detectable comic device, so any criterion bank asking 'is there wordplay / a twist / a punchline' must score them near zero; the dense side nonetheless ranks them high. R01 and R18 are the mirror image: maximum visible apparatus. This criterion is the explicit complement of construction-counting.

proposals.name: Aim turned on the speaker or reader rather than a distant target
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry implicates the writer's and reader's own side rather than mocking an out-group at a safe distance. 10 = the joke's target unmistakably includes 'us' — the speaker, the audience, or the country/community the reader belongs to — producing rueful self-recognition ('But we're we really?'; 'How Free Are You?'; 'Need To Get Out'; 'Trump might actually win.'). 5 = ambiguous aim. 0 = a named out-group is held up for ridicule from outside, with the speaker safely exempt ('Democrats America's Retarded People' aims wholly outward, as does any pure caricature of a distant type). Score direction of aim only, not political content or offensiveness in either direction.
proposals.rationale: R45, R55, R43 and R24 all convert the prompt into a question about the reader; R12 and R14 do the same in a flatter register. They share no lexical or topical feature a bank would key on, which is why the card ranks them low while the dense side ranks them high. Note R13 shows the criterion has a genuine low end within the same slice half.

proposals.name: Title substitution generates new meaning, not just phonetic proximity
proposals.instruction: For entries built by altering an existing title or slogan, score whether the alteration makes the borrowed title MEAN something about the theme. 10 = the substituted phrase reads naturally AND its new sense is a real comment on the target, so both the source and the target are illuminated. 5 = the swap is legible and pleasant but adds no claim beyond 'this word sounds like that word'. 0 = a homophone or single-letter change with no new proposition ('Judge Dread' changes spelling only; 'All the White Moves' swaps one letter and asserts nothing further), or a mashup so long that the source is buried. Entries with no borrowed title are not applicable and should be scored 5.
proposals.rationale: R19 and R29 are minimal-edit substitutions; R31 and R32 are maximal ones that graft a topical noun onto a long title without the result cohering. A bank containing 'clever wordplay' or 'creative title mashup' credits mechanical substitution wherever it appears, which plausibly drives the card's enthusiasm for the whole #GOPMovies group; this criterion grades the semantic yield of the substitution instead of its presence.

proposals.name: Decode cost: laugh requires outside lookup or niche knowledge
proposals.instruction: Score how much external knowledge a general late-night audience must already hold for the entry to resolve. 10 = fully self-resolving on first read using only common cultural stock. 5 = one moderately well-known reference, recognisable to most of the audience. 0 = the joke cannot resolve without specific niche knowledge (a decades-old film, a foreign sitcom character, a regional sports rivalry) or points outside itself to a link the reader must open. Score accessibility only; obscurity is not the same as sophistication, and a judge should not reward effortful erudition here.
proposals.rationale: R28 depends on a UK-sitcom character AND appends a URL that carries part of the payload; R31 and R32 depend on 1960s films; R30 needs a baseball rivalry supplied by a second hashtag. All are card-favoured. Any bank crediting 'specificity' or 'cultural reference' scores an obscure reference identically to an accessible one, since both are references; this criterion separates them.

proposals.name: Live-moment topicality versus archival deep cut
proposals.instruction: Score how tightly the entry is welded to the moment a reader would encounter it. 10 = engages something plainly live and unresolved at the time of writing, so the line carries present-tense charge ('Trump might actually win.'; 'Half will vote Trump.'; 'We Were Always Great'). 5 = evergreen but unforced. 0 = anchored to material that was already historical when written, so the entry could have been posted at any point in the preceding decades. Judge recency of the referenced material and the immediacy of its framing, not whether the topic is political.
proposals.rationale: R24, R12, R14 read as reports from an ongoing situation, and their charge comes from unresolved stakes rather than construction; R32 and R31 are archival by construction. A criterion bank written for general tweet quality has no temporal index, so it cannot distinguish present-tense pressure from timeless reference.

proposals.name: Transgression as sole payload versus transgression built into a construction
proposals.instruction: Score how much work remains once the taboo element is removed. 10 = the entry contains taboo material but ALSO a real construction — a coinage, a reversal, a voiced line — that would still be doing something without the shock ('That's my uncledad!' survives as a portmanteau and a spoken line). 5 = taboo plus mild framing. 0 = naming a taboo act, body part, or substance IS the entire entry, so deleting the shock leaves nothing ('Blumpkin Incest Parties'; 'raccoon penis toothpick'; 'Frenching your sister'). This criterion does not penalise offensiveness; it penalises offensiveness carrying the load alone.
proposals.rationale: R05, R47, R52, R57 are pure shock nouns and sit on the card-favoured side; R22 uses the identical taboo family but embeds it in a coinage and a voice. R41 is the instructive near-miss: same taboo, hyphen-stacked into a name rather than performed. A bank with an edginess or boldness criterion credits the shock itself, which over-credits the whole R05/R47/R52 group.

proposals.name: Dialect used as texture versus misspelling used as the target
proposals.instruction: Score how nonstandard spelling functions. 10 = phonetic or dialect spelling is the medium of a confident spoken voice, doing work no standard spelling could ('I Speak 'Merican!'; 'Y'all watch this'; 'Up the Holler'). 5 = mild dialect flavour with no particular function. 0 = the misspelling IS the joke, presented so the reader can look down at the writer's ignorance ('Forth grade thirteen-year-old'; 'Readin's For Richies'), or nonstandard spelling that appears to be an uncontrolled typo with no voice behind it. Judge the function of the orthography, not its presence.
proposals.rationale: R20, R10, R53 wield dialect from inside; R15 and R48 exhibit it from outside as the object of the joke. Both patterns satisfy any bank item about authentic voice or regional flavour, because both contain nonstandard spelling; the criterion separates inhabiting a voice from pointing at one.

proposals.name: Plays with the word-count constraint itself as comic structure
proposals.instruction: Score whether the fixed word budget is treated as material for the joke rather than as a container to fill. 10 = the count is visibly exploited — repetition that turns the budget into a rhythm, a triad that becomes a portrait, or a line whose content comments on being constrained ('Meth, Meth, Meth'; 'Moonshine, Overalls, Pickups'; 'We won't do Metric!' refusing measurement inside a counting game). 5 = fits the count naturally without engaging it. 0 = the count is met by padding, or ignored entirely. Judge structural engagement with the constraint, not mere compliance with it.
proposals.rationale: R36 and R39 are stock redneck TOPICS that nevertheless sit on the dense-favoured side, so topic novelty cannot explain them; what distinguishes them is formal use of the three-word slot. R21 does it self-referentially, and R38/R54 both convert a final slot into a duration beat. Banks typically contain a binary constraint-compliance item, which scores padding and structure alike.

proposals.name: Scans as a clean spoken beat when read aloud
proposals.instruction: Score the prosody of the line spoken at conversational speed. 10 = a crisp rhythmic unit with a stressed final syllable that lands, no awkward clusters, easy to say in one breath ('NASCAR and Chill'; 'Road kill buffet'; 'Pass the ammunition'). 5 = sayable but rhythmically flat. 0 = a mouthful requiring re-reading, with stumbling clusters, stacked modifiers, or a trailing tail that drains the ending ('Harold and Kumar Return to Guantanamo Bay'; 'What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?'). Judge sound and rhythm only; a semantically weak line can score 10 here.
proposals.rationale: The dense-favoured half is systematically shorter and end-stressed (R33, R23, R49, R42), the card-favoured half systematically longer and trailing (R60, R32, R18). Written criterion banks are built from semantic properties and rarely encode delivery rhythm, so a well-constructed but unspeakable line scores full marks on the card.

proposals.name: Crowdedness: how many entrants would independently produce this move
proposals.instruction: Estimate how obvious this move is given the prompt. 10 = a specific, personal, or oblique angle unlikely to be duplicated by another entrant. 5 = a familiar angle with an individual execution. 0 = the single most predictable association with the hashtag, executed in the most predictable way, such that dozens of entrants would submit a near-identical line. A judge should ask: if a hundred people answered this prompt, how many produce essentially this? Score only predictability of the move; a crowded move can still be competently written.
proposals.rationale: The slice contains direct evidence of duplication: R25 and R58 are the same Jar Jar joke twice, R17 is a third Star Wars answer to the same prompt, and R27 and R47 both reach for a raccoon; all five sit on the card-favoured side. A criterion bank judges each item in isolation and therefore cannot see that the move is crowded, which is precisely the quantity a model trained across the whole pool would internalise.

proposals.name: Stops on the beat: no explanation, parenthetical, or hedging second joke
proposals.instruction: Score restraint after the punchline. 10 = the entry ends exactly at the funny word, with nothing appended ('Tell you what.'; 'Up the Holler'). 5 = a slight tail that does no damage. 0 = the joke is followed by material that explains it, insures it, or adds a second attempt — a clarifying parenthetical ('16 Angry Men (and one woman)'), an appended tag supplying the missing context ('...#STLCards'), a link, or a redundant final clause. Judge only what follows the punchline.
proposals.rationale: R18, R30, R28 each append the explanation that a confident version would omit, and R60 keeps going past its own joke; the dense-favoured lines characteristically stop (R44, R53, R42). Banks reward the presence of context and completeness, so an explanatory tail reads to the card as added information rather than as a leak of confidence.

proposals.name: Tag-first layout: handle and hashtag precede the joke span
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT to which contest metadata occupies the start of the text. 10 = the text opens with '@midnight' and/or the contest hashtag and the reader passes through all metadata before the first content word. 5 = metadata is interleaved, e.g. one tag leads and another trails, or the hashtag leads while the handle trails. 0 = the text opens directly on content and all handles/hashtags are at the end. Count only WHERE the tokens sit, not what they say. Do NOT judge whether leading or trailing is better, funnier, or more competent; a judge who finds themselves forming an opinion about delivery has left this channel.
proposals.rationale: This layout separates the slice almost mechanically: R06, R07, R09, R10, R21 and R51 all open with '@midnight', while R02, R03, R08, R23 and R25 open on content. Nothing about the joke changes if the tags move, so as a channel it is pure position. It is tagged mixed because the same underlying habit -- writing in the compose box, treating the entry as a crafted line -- could plausibly also produce genuinely better entries, so it must appear in both readouts.
proposals.upstream_parent: posting interface and posting habit (replying inside the @midnight thread versus composing a fresh tweet), which tracks how routinely the author plays this format

proposals.name: Non-authored mechanical residue: whitespace runs, entities, shortened URLs
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT of tokens and spacing that no author would deliberately type as part of a joke. Count: runs of two or more consecutive spaces; HTML entities appearing as literal text ('&'); t.co or other shortened URLs; stray leading/trailing spacing; any encoding debris. 10 = several such artifacts present. 5 = exactly one mild artifact, such as a single double-space. 0 = clean single-spaced text with no entities or links. Score presence and quantity only. Do NOT treat artifacts as sloppiness or as evidence of care; this channel is a measure of transport residue, not of the writer.
proposals.rationale: R13 carries four literal '&' sequences and R38 carries a trailing t.co link; R05, R11, R44 and R55 all carry internal double-spaces. These marks are produced by the pipeline and the compose client rather than by the joke, yet they are perfectly visible to a text-only model and could be picked up as signal. The artifact rate plausibly differs by client and by capture date, which is exactly the kind of correlation that must never enter a criterion bank.
proposals.upstream_parent: the client used to compose plus the scrape/encoding pipeline that captured the tweet (hashtag autocomplete inserting spaces; attachments and quote-links; entity escaping at ingestion)

proposals.name: House-style tag fidelity and absence of off-contest hashtags
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT to which the entry's tagging matches the contest's canonical form. 10 = the contest hashtag appears exactly once, in the canonical camel-case rendering, with no additional hashtags and no variant spelling. 5 = one deviation, e.g. altered casing. 0 = multiple deviations: extra hashtags beyond the contest tag, non-canonical casing, or the tag rendered differently from the on-air form. Score conformity of the tagging only. Do NOT judge whether conformity indicates skill, and do NOT let the joke's content influence the score.
proposals.rationale: R12 renders the tag as '#GOPmovies' rather than the canonical camel case, and R41 appends an off-contest '#STLCards' that also smuggles in context. Conformity here is a fingerprint of repeat participation rather than of the entry's merit, but it is tagged mixed because a repeat entrant may also genuinely write better entries, so discounting it could remove real signal along with the nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's accumulated practice in this specific nightly format (whether they have played before and internalised its conventions)

proposals.name: Casing convention of the joke span
proposals.instruction: Classify and score the EXTENT of capitalisation applied to the content words (ignore hashtags and handles). 10 = every content word is capitalised, Title Case throughout. 6 = ordinary sentence case with an initial capital. 3 = inconsistent or partial capitalisation. 0 = entirely lowercase content. Score the convention only. Do NOT judge whether any convention looks more polished, more emphatic or more amateur, and do NOT reason about what the casing implies about the writer.
proposals.rationale: Title Case runs through R03, R27, R37 and R59, while fully lowercase content appears in R29 and R40. Casing is an author-level constant that would be identical across every entry that author ever submits, so it cannot be a property of this entry's quality, yet it is one of the most learnable surface regularities in the text and is therefore a prime candidate for a text-only model to exploit.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's habitual composition style and input device (mobile autocapitalisation, Title Case as a stylistic default), a stable per-author trait unrelated to any single entry

proposals.name: Shouted emphasis: all-caps words and exclamation marks
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT of typographic shouting in the content span. Count fully capitalised words that are not acronyms or proper nouns, plus exclamation marks, plus any other emphatic typography. 10 = an all-caps word AND an exclamation mark, or multiple instances of either. 5 = one instance. 0 = neither present. Acronyms and brand names in caps (for example NASCAR) do not count. Score frequency only. Do NOT judge whether the emphasis is well placed, earned, or funny.
proposals.rationale: Emphatic typography is markedly concentrated on one side of the slice: R05 and R11 both end on a capitalised 'FOREVER', R08 shouts 'NECK!', and R17, R28, R30 and R59 each carry an exclamation or an all-caps word. A model can key on the presence of a caps run without any access to whether the emphasis lands, which makes this an easily learned proxy that no criterion bank should be allowed to adopt.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Raw length of the content span excluding tags
proposals.instruction: Measure the EXTENT of text once handles, hashtags and URLs are stripped. Score inversely by length: 10 = very short, roughly three words or under twenty characters. 5 = moderate, roughly five to seven words. 0 = long, roughly eight or more words or over forty-five characters. Count only; do not read for meaning. Do NOT judge whether the length is appropriate to the prompt, whether the entry is tight or padded, or whether brevity suits the joke. This channel is a ruler, not a critic.
proposals.rationale: The two halves separate strongly by raw length: R04 and R34 run to seven and eight content words, R13 packs five conjoined names, while R23, R25 and R47 are three words apiece. Length is trivially computable and would be learned by any text-only model, but it is tagged mixed because in a contest that specifies a word count, compression is arguably part of the craft, so the discounted and undiscounted readouts should bracket it rather than one of them deciding it.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing effort and revision before posting, plus how much of the character budget the author felt obliged to fill

proposals.name: Proper-noun and borrowed-title load
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT to which the content consists of named entities imported from outside: film and show titles, brand names, celebrity or character names, franchise names. 10 = the content is essentially an imported title or a chain of proper nouns with minimal original wording. 5 = one named entity embedded in otherwise original wording. 0 = no proper nouns at all. Count density of borrowed names only. Do NOT judge whether the reference is apt, well known, well transformed, or funny; a brilliant use and a lazy use of the same name score identically here.
proposals.rationale: Reference load tracks the split closely: R13, R22, R34, R54 and R60 are built almost entirely from imported titles and names, while R25, R23, R27 and R48 contain none. Because entity density is partly a property of the PROMPT rather than of the entry, it can carry contest-level structure into an item-level score. It is tagged mixed since a well-chosen reference can be real craft.
proposals.upstream_parent: which contest prompt was drawn that night (some prompts invite title mashups, others invite original phrasing) together with the author's habit of reaching for a reference bank

proposals.name: Taboo, anatomical and intoxicant lexical load
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT of shock vocabulary present, regardless of how it is used. Count explicit sexual terms, anatomical terms, incest or assault references, and named drugs. 10 = the content is composed mainly of such terms. 5 = one such term inside otherwise neutral content. 0 = none present. Score lexical presence and density only. Do NOT judge whether the transgression is earned, gratuitous, funny or offensive, and do NOT adjust for how well it is deployed; this channel deliberately cannot tell a good taboo joke from a bad one.
proposals.rationale: R21, R40, R49, R10 and R51 cluster this vocabulary densely on one side of the slice, and R20 sits alongside them. Because the same taboo material appears on the other side too (R42), density plainly does not track construction quality, yet it is a highly learnable lexical signature. It is tagged not-mixed because the conjectured parent -- which corner of the audience the author is playing to -- is a property of the venue, not of the entry.
proposals.upstream_parent: the sub-audience and venue register the author is writing toward (late-night edgy stream norms and who is submitting into them), rather than anything about this entry's construction

proposals.name: Subject domain: national-media-political versus domestic-regional material
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT to which the content draws on national political and mass-media material rather than domestic, regional or household material. 10 = entirely national-political or mass-media (parties, politicians, legislation, films, franchises). 5 = mixed or neutral. 0 = entirely domestic or regional (family, food, vehicles, animals, local place-texture). Score subject matter only. Do NOT judge whether the domain suits the prompt, and do NOT let the wit of the treatment shift the score.
proposals.rationale: Domain and slice-side are heavily entangled: the media-political items R13, R34, R50, R53 and R56 group together, while the domestic-regional items R19, R23, R46 and R47 group opposite. Since every entry under one hashtag shares the same domain pressure, an item-level score that keys on domain is partly scoring which night the entry came from. Tagged mixed because the prompt genuinely constrains what a good entry looks like, so the effect cannot be cleanly excised.
proposals.upstream_parent: which contest prompt was drawn and what that night's audience and news cycle supplied; the prompt is a container-level variable shared by every entry submitted under it

proposals.name: First-reading obviousness: reads as an early, most-available take
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT to which the entry reads like one of the first associations anyone would produce on seeing the prompt, versus a riff that presupposes the obvious takes are already gone. 10 = the single most available association, phrased in the most available way, of a kind you would expect many entrants to arrive at independently. 5 = a familiar angle with some individual turn. 0 = the entry visibly presupposes prior entries -- it comments on the contest medium itself, corrects or one-ups an implied earlier take, or reaches for an angle only available after the obvious ones are exhausted. Score availability of the move only. Do NOT judge whether obviousness or lateness is better; an obvious take can be superbly written and a late riff can be strained.
proposals.rationale: The slice itself contains direct evidence of the ordering effect: R22, R54 and R60 are three separate Star Wars answers to the same prompt, R40 and R57 both reach for a raccoon, and R20, R21 and R49 all reach for incest -- the signature of a crowded container where the same associations arrive repeatedly. Against these, R35 jokes about the act of tweeting itself and R59 corrects an implied prior reference ('ACTUAL Sister Wives'), both moves that presuppose a stream already in progress. A text-only model scoring this fingerprint is partly scoring WHEN an entry arrived, not how good it is; tagged mixed because arriving at a non-obvious angle is also plausibly real craft.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream and submission timing (how many entries the author had already seen when composing), which is invisible in the text but leaves an availability fingerprint

proposals.name: Deadpan slogan authenticity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet reads exactly like a genuine, unforced slogan, saying, or found-phrase that could plausibly exist independent of any joke-writing process, with no visible pun mechanics, wordplay signaling, or exaggerated comic diction. Score 0 if the tweet is obviously constructed as a joke, with visible punchline machinery, wordplay, or theatrical comic phrasing.
proposals.rationale: Dense ranks deadpan, slogan-style entries far above the scorecard (R05 'We Were Always Great' dense_pct=.988 vs card_pct=.250; R28 'We won't do Metric!' dense_pct=.993 vs card_pct=.336; R16 'The 4th of July' dense_pct=.713 vs card_pct=.162), suggesting dense rewards unforced authenticity that a criteria-bank scorecard, built to detect explicit joke devices, does not credit.

proposals.name: Political-figure/current-event audacity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet directly names a real, currently contested political figure, party, or event and stakes out a blunt, unhedged opinion about it. Score 0 if the tweet avoids all real-world political specificity and controversy.
proposals.rationale: Dense ranks politically pointed entries much higher than the scorecard does (R27 'Democrats America's Retarded People' dense_pct=.846 vs card_pct=.022, the largest dense-over-card gap in the slice; R14 'Trump might actually win.' dense_pct=.750 vs card_pct=.199; R02 'Half will vote Trump.' dense_pct=.752 vs card_pct=.233), suggesting the scorecard's criteria discount or actively penalize partisan bluntness that dense treats as comedic value.

proposals.name: Extreme word-count economy for the concept
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the entry conveys its full comic concept in the fewest possible words, with zero filler, qualifiers, or setup. Score 0 if the entry uses more words than the concept requires, including unnecessary framing or explanation.
proposals.rationale: Dense favors terse 2-4 word entries that the scorecard underrates (R13 'Married My Truck' dense_pct=.983 vs card_pct=.480; R47 'Road kill buffet' dense_pct=.858 vs card_pct=.353; R59 'Tell you what.' dense_pct=.740 vs card_pct=.238), suggesting the scorecard is not crediting maximal compression as a virtue in itself.

proposals.name: Precision pun on one specific known title
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the entry takes one specific, identifiable existing title (movie, show, or song) and alters exactly the minimal words needed to create a clear, legible twist tied to the contest theme. Score 0 if there is no identifiable source title being punned, or the alteration is too vague to recognize a specific source.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard strongly favors sharp single-title puns that dense underrates (R30 'Crouching Hairpiece Hidden Agenda' card_pct=.988 vs dense_pct=.086; R41 'Kill Bill of Rights' card_pct=.936 vs dense_pct=.029; R23 'Dude, Where Are My Votes?' card_pct=.978 vs dense_pct=.390), suggesting the scorecard rewards recognizable pun mechanics that dense weights less heavily.

proposals.name: Verbatim borrowing without transformation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the entry quotes or nearly quotes an existing famous phrase, slogan, or title with little to no wording change, relying on audience recognition of the source rather than any original twist. Score 0 if the entry is composed of original wording with no identifiable pre-existing source being quoted.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard rates some near-verbatim borrowings surprisingly high relative to dense (R18 'Tastes great, less filling', the Miller Lite slogan almost unchanged, card_pct=.963 vs dense_pct=.233; R11 'Harold and Kumar Return to Guantanamo Bay' card_pct=.748 vs dense_pct=.159), suggesting the scorecard rewards recognizability/fluency even absent real transformation, something dense discounts.

proposals.name: Graphic/visceral taboo imagery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the entry describes a taboo, transgressive, or gross-out subject with vivid, specific, sensory physical detail (texture, body part, act). Score 0 if any taboo content present is only referenced abstractly or euphemistically with no sensory specificity.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard rates viscerally graphic entries far above dense (R06 'Great grandmas moist moose knuckle.' card_pct=.902 vs dense_pct=.277; R37 'raccoon penis toothpick' card_pct=.819 vs dense_pct=.221; R10 'Family reunion Rohypnol' card_pct=.973 vs dense_pct=.164), suggesting the scorecard credits explicit, visceral description that dense does not reward to the same degree.

proposals.name: Specific real-world proper-noun anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the entry names a specific, real, dated proper noun (a named person, company, sports team, or news event) central to the joke. Score 0 if the entry uses only generic categories or unnamed stereotypes with no specific real-world referent.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard favors entries anchored to specific real referents that dense undervalues (R56 'Taco Bell owns Chipolte now.' card_pct=.775 vs dense_pct=.196; R21 'Cubs Win the World Series' card_pct=.865 vs dense_pct=.223; R25 '...Kim Davis' card_pct=.760 vs dense_pct=.020), suggesting named-entity specificity is scorecard-rewarded but comparatively invisible to dense.

proposals.name: Strict adherence to the hashtag's literal format
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the entry is built precisely to the letter of the contest's stated constraint (e.g., phrased exactly as a movie title for a movies hashtag). Score 0 if the entry only loosely gestures at the theme without matching its literal format.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard favors entries with tight format fidelity to #GOP_Movies' movie-title convention that dense ranks low (R03 'All the White Moves' card_pct=.826 vs dense_pct=.081; R04 'What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?' card_pct=.694 vs dense_pct=.132; R09 '16 Angry Men (and one woman)' card_pct=.846 vs dense_pct=.113), suggesting the scorecard's rubric rewards format compliance more than dense does.

proposals.name: Delayed double-meaning / second-read click
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the entry supports two distinct simultaneous readings such that the second, hidden meaning only becomes clear on a re-read, producing a delayed comic realization. Score 0 if the entry has exactly one flat, immediately apparent meaning with no ambiguity.
proposals.rationale: Dense rewards entries with layered ambiguity that the scorecard underrates (R55 'But we're we really?' dense_pct=.956 vs card_pct=.039, the second-largest dense-over-card gap in the slice; R33 'That's my uncledad!' dense_pct=.855 vs card_pct=.091), suggesting the scorecard's item-by-item criteria miss ambiguity that only appears on careful re-read.

proposals.name: In-character dialect/phonetic voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the entry is written using the stereotyped group's spoken vernacular, phonetic spelling, or regional idiom (e.g., dropped letters, colloquial contractions) as an integral part of the joke's persona. Score 0 if the entry is written in unmarked standard English with no dialect signaling.
proposals.rationale: Dialect-voiced entries appear on both sides of the disagreement (R08 'I Speak 'Merican!' dense_pct=.929 vs card_pct=.387; R54 'Up the Holler' dense_pct=.961 vs card_pct=.377; R48 'Forth grade thirteen-year-old' card_pct=.855 vs dense_pct=.257), suggesting voice/persona construction is weighted very differently by the two models and is not currently isolated as its own property.

proposals.name: Self-referential joke about the tweet/platform itself
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the joke's premise is about the act of tweeting, the account, the hashtag contest mechanics, or the platform itself, rather than the nominal external theme. Score 0 if the entry makes no reference to the tweeting/platform context at all.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard rewards meta/platform-referential entries that dense undervalues (R50 'Tweeted from the wrong account' card_pct=.892 vs dense_pct=.319; R20 'David Brent in porn flick', which foregrounds the tweet as an object by including a live link, card_pct=.610 vs dense_pct=.022), a self-reflexive property not otherwise named.

proposals.name: Parallel list/catalog construction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the punchline is built as a short list of 2-4 parallel nouns or short phrases rather than a single clause. Score 0 if the entry is a single unified clause with no list structure.
proposals.rationale: List-structured entries appear on both sides of the gap (R52 'Moonshine, Overalls, Pickups' dense_pct=.934 vs card_pct=.071; R32 'Corn syrup and salt' card_pct=.755 vs dense_pct=.071), indicating list/catalog form is a structurally distinct property driving disagreement independent of content.

proposals.name: Rhetorical question framing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the entry is phrased as a question that invites the reader to supply or infer the punchline rather than stating it outright. Score 0 if the entry is a flat declarative statement with no interrogative framing.
proposals.rationale: Dense rewards question-framed entries that the scorecard misses (R49 'How Free Are You?' dense_pct=.958 vs card_pct=.363; R55 'But we're we really?' dense_pct=.956 vs card_pct=.039), suggesting interrogative construction is an under-recognized comic device.

proposals.name: Franchise-fatigue / sequel-exhaustion meta-joke
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the joke's content specifically comments on a franchise, series, or format being over-extended, running out of ideas, or reaching an absurd Nth installment. Score 0 if the entry contains no commentary on repetition, sequels, or franchise longevity.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard favors franchise-fatigue jokes that dense underrates (R22 'Star Wars VII: series finale' card_pct=.939 vs dense_pct=.135; R36 'Jar Jar Binks spin-off movie.' card_pct=.904 vs dense_pct=.172; R38 'Star Wars 7 With JarJar.' card_pct=.848 vs dense_pct=.275), a specific, recurring comic target not otherwise named.

proposals.name: Disproportionate consequence-escalation absurdity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the joke takes a mundane, low-stakes premise and escalates its stated consequence to an absurdly disproportionate extreme (e.g., permanence, infinity, irreversibility). Score 0 if the stated consequence is proportionate and mundane with no escalation.
proposals.rationale: Dense rewards escalation-to-extreme entries that the scorecard misses (R43 'Mother visits me, stays FOREVER' dense_pct=.966 vs card_pct=.213; R60 'Wifi was shut off, FOREVER' dense_pct=.880 vs card_pct=.294), pointing to a specific comic escalation mechanic not currently captured.

proposals.name: Boilerplate tag placed before vs. after the punchline
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the required boilerplate (the @midnight handle and/or the contest hashtag) appears BEFORE the joke's content words rather than after. 10 = all boilerplate (handle and hashtag) precedes the punchline text; 0 = all boilerplate follows the punchline text, which appears first. This is an extent measure of ordering only -- do not judge whether the entry is funny or well-written.
proposals.rationale: Leading-boilerplate ordering is heavily concentrated in the card-favored half (R02, R09, R16, R18, R20, R22, R27, R33, R34, R35, R44, R53 all place @midnight and/or the hashtag before the joke text), while trailing-boilerplate ordering is heavily concentrated in the dense-favored half (R01, R05, R11, R21, R37, R54, R57 all place the joke text first). This near-categorical split tracks a formatting/provenance habit, not joke quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: curation/provenance pipeline (which scrape or compiled list the item was drawn from) and/or author's routine practice of appending vs. prepending required tags

proposals.name: Trailing or leading single-word ALL-CAPS emphasis
proposals.instruction: Score how much the entry uses a single word rendered in ALL CAPS purely for emphasis (not an acronym). 10 = a clear emphasis word in full caps is present; 0 = no capitalized emphasis word anywhere. Do not judge whether the emphasis is effective or funny.
proposals.rationale: This typographic tic recurs on the dense-favored side (R12 'stays FOREVER', R24 'stays FOREVER', R57 'My NECK!') and is a capitalization habit rather than a property of the joke's content.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Terminal exclamation mark vs. terminal period
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the entry ends on an exclamation mark as opposed to a period or no terminal punctuation. 10 = ends in '!'; 0 = ends in '.' or no punctuation at all. Score only the punctuation mark present, not the entry's energy or quality.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored entries disproportionately end in '!' (R01 'Texas!', R14 'uncledad!', R28 ''Merican!', R54 'Metric!'), while card-favored entries disproportionately end in a flat period (R08 'movie.', R17 'knuckle.', R55 'now.'), a pure punctuation-choice difference.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Raw word/character count of the entry body
proposals.instruction: Score how long the entry is in raw word count, independent of content. 10 = among the longest entries in this set (8+ words); 0 = among the shortest (2-3 words). Do not judge whether the length suits the joke.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored entries cluster short (R58 'Married My Truck', R51 'Need To Get Out'), while several card-favored entries run much longer (R44 'What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?', R36 'Bob & Ted & Carol & Alice & Kim Davis'), so raw length alone tracks the disagreement even though brevity could also be a genuine stylistic virtue.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Bare noun-phrase construction with no finite verb
proposals.instruction: Score how much the entry is a bare noun phrase or list of nouns with no conjugated verb, as opposed to a full clause with a subject and verb. 10 = pure noun phrase, no verb; 0 = a complete sentence with a finite verb. Score grammatical form only.
proposals.rationale: Several dense-favored entries are verb-less noun phrases (R38 'Road kill buffet', R41 'Moonshine, Overalls, Pickups', R29 'Up the Holler'), a template plausibly learned through repeated practice in this exact contest format rather than a property of the joke's wit -- though practiced entrants may also simply write better jokes.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's seniority/practice in this specific contest format (regulars learn to strip entries to noun phrases)

proposals.name: Genericness of the theme association (first-guess reading)
proposals.instruction: Score how generic and predictable the entry's connection to the hashtag's theme is, independent of whether it is funny. 10 = the single most obvious, first-thing-anyone-would-say association with the theme, a cultural cliche with no twist; 0 = an oblique, multi-reference, or highly specific construction nobody would guess as a first attempt. Do not judge quality, only predictability of the association.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored entries skew toward maximally generic, cliche associations (R01 'God Bless Texas!', R43 'The 4th of July'), while card-favored entries skew toward elaborate multi-reference constructions that read like later, more effortful riffs after the obvious ground was taken (R36 'Bob & Ted & Carol & Alice & Kim Davis', R18 'Crouching Hairpiece Hidden Agenda'). This plausibly fingerprints early-obvious vs. late-riff position in the submission stream, though a widely shared cliche could also be genuinely funny via broad recognition.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream / submission timing (obvious associations get claimed early; oblique ones emerge from later entrants who have already seen the obvious takes taken)

proposals.name: Apparent unintentional spelling or grammar error
proposals.instruction: Score how much the entry contains a visible, apparently unintentional spelling or grammar error (misspelled word, wrong homophone, subject-verb mismatch). 10 = a clear error is present; 0 = no apparent error. Do not judge whether the error is charming or detracts.
proposals.rationale: Typos appear on both sides of the split and are plausibly submission-haste artifacts rather than joke content (R59 'Forth grade' for 'Fourth grade', card-favored; R55 'Chipolte' for 'Chipotle', card-favored; R42 'But we're we really?', dense-favored, likely intended 'where').
proposals.upstream_parent: editing effort / haste at submission (typed quickly on a phone, no proofreading pass, or autocorrect interference)

proposals.name: Generic standalone-tweet 'quotable' register
proposals.instruction: Score how much the entry reads as a generically shareable, quotable standalone tweet that would make sense and could plausibly get engagement even completely outside this specific contest, versus an entry that only makes sense as a move inside this specific contest's rules. 10 = reads as a fully generic, shareable one-liner with no contest-specific mechanics; 0 = only functions given the exact hashtag/game constraint. Score only how self-contained/generic the phrasing is, not its wit.
proposals.rationale: Several dense-favored entries read as tweets that could stand entirely on their own outside the game (R01 'God Bless Texas!', R37 'We Were Always Great', R52 'How Free Are You?'), which may reflect a general 'good tweet' prior in the dense model rather than fit to this specific contest -- though broadly appealing phrasing could also be a genuinely strong entry.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's general social-media following-building practice / writing for broad engagement rather than this specific game's internal rules

proposals.name: Contest sub-hashtag category membership
proposals.instruction: Score, purely categorically, how much this entry belongs to the #GOP_Movies sub-format versus the other three sub-formats (#Redneck_In_3_Words, #America_In_4_Words, #Scary_Story_In_5_Words). 10 = a #GOP_Movies entry; 0 = any of the other three. This is a category-membership marker only, not a judgment of the entry's execution.
proposals.rationale: Card-favored status is heavily concentrated in #GOP_Movies entries (R02, R09, R16, R18, R20, R22, R36, R44, R53 are all card-favored #GOP_Movies items), while #Redneck_In_3_Words items are disproportionately dense-favored (R01, R11, R58), suggesting the two rubrics may simply be differentially legible across sub-formats rather than tracking execution quality within each.
proposals.upstream_parent: differential structural legibility of the two rubrics to each contest sub-format (movie-title-matching genre vs. slogan/stereotype genre)

proposals.name: Informal contraction / spoken-voice apostrophe density
proposals.instruction: Score how many informal contractions (e.g., don't, that's, won't, y'all) appear in the entry. 10 = multiple contractions present, reading as casual spoken voice; 0 = no contractions, fully formal wording. Score contraction density only, not tone quality.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored entries are noticeably contraction-heavy (R05 'Don't stop me now.', R14 'That's my uncledad!', R23 'Y'all watch this', R54 'We won't do Metric!'), a lexical/orthographic register marker distinct from -- but plausibly correlated with -- the joke's underlying authenticity.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's register choice (formal vs. informal spoken-voice writing style)

proposals.name: Concrete visuality
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the wording instantly creates a vivid, specific physical scene; give 0 when it remains abstract, generic, or visually ungrounded.
proposals.rationale: R08, R45, and R58 stage memorable physical situations with very few words, unlike many merely topical or titular entries.

proposals.name: Implied backstory
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when a short line strongly implies a specific preceding situation or relationship; give 0 when it communicates no situation beyond its literal wording.
proposals.rationale: R03, R37, and R49 invite the reader to reconstruct an entire unsettling or comic story from a compressed premise.

proposals.name: Idiomatic repurposing
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when a familiar conversational phrase is naturally redirected toward the hashtag premise; give 0 when wording is literal, stiff, or merely clichéd.
proposals.rationale: R06, R16, R32, and R57 use recognizable spoken phrases whose ordinary cadence becomes contextually comic.

proposals.name: Expectation reversal
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the ending sharply overturns the interpretation established at the beginning; give 0 when the line has no meaningful turn.
proposals.rationale: R03, R36, and R60 pivot from an ordinary setup to an unexpectedly dark, absurd, or culturally specific reading.

proposals.name: Conversational performability
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the line sounds effortless spoken aloud, with clear rhythm, emphasis, and timing; give 0 when it sounds like a noun pile or written label.
proposals.rationale: R06, R16, R25, and R57 have strong spoken cadence, whereas entries such as R14 and R35 read more like assembled text.

proposals.name: Information density
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when nearly every word supplies necessary comic context or escalation; give 0 when wording is padded, redundant, or too underdeveloped to support a premise.
proposals.rationale: R29, R45, and R49 pack stance, context, and imagery into compact lines without explanatory filler.

proposals.name: Unexpected combination
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when two familiar concepts form a surprising but immediately interpretable combination; give 0 when the pairing is predictable or merely a stock list.
proposals.rationale: R08, R36, and R60 create fresh collisions between familiar concepts, while R01 and R22 rely more on predictable category associations.

proposals.name: Prompt-specific transformation
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the hashtag constraint transforms the material into a new comic angle; give 0 when the text simply lists a stereotype or repeats a generic slogan fitting the prompt.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R45 turn redneck associations into premises, while R01, R22, R35, and R44 mainly supply literal or stock prompt material.

proposals.name: Specific comic consequence
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the text clearly identifies an action, relationship, or consequence that makes the joke concrete; give 0 when it offers only a vague assertion or topic.
proposals.rationale: R03, R45, and R49 establish precise relationships or consequences, unlike broad assertions such as R42 and R48.

proposals.name: Shock independence
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the joke remains substantially funny after its taboo or grossest term is mentally removed; give 0 when provocation is essentially the entire mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R02, R07, R23, R40, and R47 depend heavily on sexual, bodily, or taboo shock with little additional comic structure.

proposals.name: Reference integration
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when an outside cultural reference is transformed into a self-contained joke; give 0 when it is merely pasted, stacked, or used as an unexplained title reference.
proposals.rationale: R05 integrates a movie title into a political premise, while R09, R31, R33, and R51 mostly invoke recognizable titles without comparable transformation.

proposals.name: Natural wordplay
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when a pun preserves grammatical naturalness while creating a precise new meaning; give 0 when it is a forced title substitution, loose rhyme, or strained phonetic gimmick.
proposals.rationale: R36, R49, and R60 make their wordplay function as readable premises, unlike the more mechanically substituted constructions in R12, R24, R34, and R56.

proposals.name: Distinctive point of view
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the wording expresses a vivid, unmistakable speaker attitude or persona; give 0 when it is neutral inventory, generic description, or impersonal slogan.
proposals.rationale: R17, R25, and R42 communicate strong attitudes, whereas R35 and R44 present broadly reusable slogans without much individual voice.

proposals.name: Cultural stakes
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the line invokes a recognizable social or political tension with a clear stance; give 0 when it merely mentions a topic without conflict or pressure.
proposals.rationale: R18, R29, and R42 embed conflict over identity, national habits, or politics, while R35 and R44 are comparatively generic cultural references.

proposals.name: Purposeful linguistic deviation
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when unusual spelling, grammar, or word formation itself creates comic meaning or persona; give 0 when the deviation appears accidental, distracting, or irrelevant.
proposals.rationale: R10 and R49 use altered language to signal voice and identity, whereas the errors or malformed phrases in R28 and R56 do not clearly add a comic mechanism.

proposals.name: Prompt-language echo
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the substantive text repeats or closely evokes the contest prompt's wording or semantic frame, excluding the required hashtag and handle; judge only presence, never whether the reuse is good.
proposals.rationale: Prompt-framing echoes appear in the Fourth-of-July/America wording of R11 and the explicit America wording of R29, and in the neck reference of R33. Such topical overlap can be predictive while remaining separate from entry quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Regional stereotype props
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains recognizable regional-stereotype objects, activities, or vernacular; judge only extent, never whether the stereotype is good or funny.
proposals.rationale: R47 lists moonshine, overalls, and pickups, while R60 invokes NASCAR and R25 invokes a truck. A dense cluster of culturally stereotyped props can attract text-based associations without being an intrinsic quality criterion.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Taboo shock lexicon
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text uses sexual, bodily, incestuous, drug-related, or otherwise taboo vocabulary; judge only lexical presence, never whether its use is good.
proposals.rationale: R20, R30, R36, and R40 contain sexual or incestuous terms, while R54 repeats a drug term. Taboo vocabulary is a salient textual signal that can distort judgments independently of contest quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Named-reference density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the amount of recognizable proper names, films, franchises, celebrities, politicians, teams, or other external cultural references; judge only density, never whether the references are good.
proposals.rationale: R09 references Baby Jane and healthcare, and R49, R51, and R53 rework recognizable film titles or cultural names. External-reference density can be predictive through familiarity and association rather than entry quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Orthographic irregularity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of misspellings, grammatical anomalies, malformed plurals, or unusual word forms visible in the text; judge only the irregularities, never whether they improve the entry.
proposals.rationale: R13 has a duplicated or malformed phrase, R27 has 'Forth' and an awkward noun phrase, and R55 misspells 'Chipotle.' Such irregularities can become model-visible nuisance signals without constituting a quality dimension.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Emphasis typography
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of all-caps words, conspicuous capitalization, repeated punctuation, or emphatic typographic styling; judge only amount, never whether the emphasis is good.
proposals.rationale: R17 emphasizes FOREVER, R28 emphasizes ACTUAL, and R33 emphasizes NECK with capitals and punctuation. These visual salience cues can influence text processing independently of the underlying joke.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Contest-wrapper arrangement
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the required contest hashtag and @midnight handle appear in a standardized, boilerplate-like order, spacing, or adjacency pattern; judge only formatting extent, never whether the arrangement is good.
proposals.rationale: R03 places the handle and hashtag before the text, whereas R36 places the hashtag and handle before the text in a different wrapper pattern; R01 places both after the text. A receiving or platform formatting convention could leave these textual fingerprints without describing quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: receiving-side process

proposals.name: Format-fluent slogan style
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the substantive text uses compressed, idiomatic, slogan-like, or telegraphic phrasing associated with practiced hashtag-contest participation; judge only the construction's presence, never whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: R08, R38, and R46 use compact idiomatic constructions such as 'Pass the ammunition,' 'Y'all watch this,' and 'Tell you what.' An author's practice in this format could produce this fingerprint and could also genuinely improve writing, so it is mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format

proposals.name: Audience-facing residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains optional audience-facing material beyond the contest wrapper, such as extra hashtags, external links, affiliations, or targeting cues; judge only amount, never whether the outreach is good.
proposals.rationale: R34 adds the audience-affiliation hashtag #STLCards, and R43 includes an external link. Audience or following dynamics could produce these visible residues and affect textual treatment without being a criterion for contest quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience/following

proposals.name: Continuation-riff framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text signals a sequel, spin-off, return, finale, continuation, or modification of an already-known premise; judge only the framing extent, never whether the riff is fresh or good.
proposals.rationale: R15 uses 'series finale,' R21 uses 'spin-off movie,' and R48 modifies Star Wars with JarJar. A late position in a crowded entry stream could leave this derivative or second-order fingerprint; that timing might also affect genuine idea development, so it is mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Hashtag-specific reframing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the prompt is reinterpreted through an unexpected, tightly fitting premise; score 0 when the response is a literal or generic association.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R06 turn their prompts into surprising premises rather than merely listing familiar associations.

proposals.name: Sound-and-spelling wordplay
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a deliberate sound, spelling, or segmentation shift creates an immediate second reading; score 0 when wording has no such transformation.
proposals.rationale: R02 uses solar/redneck sound play, while R26 compresses uncle and dad into uncledad.

proposals.name: Implied mini-narrative
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a few words imply characters, action, and consequence; score 0 when they are disconnected labels or nouns.
proposals.rationale: R23 implies an unsettling visit that never ends, and R51 implies a damaging posting mistake.

proposals.name: Concrete sensory imagery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording creates a specific, easily pictured scene with concrete objects or sensations; score 0 when it remains abstract or generic.
proposals.rationale: R05 supplies a vivid cluster of moonshine, overalls, and pickups, while R58 creates a grotesque buffet image.

proposals.name: Role reversal or personification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an animal or object takes on a recognizably human social role in a coherent joke; score 0 when entities behave conventionally.
proposals.rationale: R06 makes a truck a spouse, and R30 makes a dog a vehicle copilot.

proposals.name: Productive double reading
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording supports two plausible interpretations whose tension creates the humor; score 0 when only one unambiguous meaning is available.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R09 use deliberately open phrasing that can be read both literally and politically.

proposals.name: Ominous permanence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary event is made funny or frightening by an irreversible, absolute, or excessively permanent consequence; score 0 when consequences are temporary or absent.
proposals.rationale: R23 turns a mother's visit into forever, while R35 makes an everyday internet interruption permanent.

proposals.name: Performed conversational voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when diction and cadence vividly perform a recognizable speaker or spoken moment; score 0 when the wording sounds like an impersonal label.
proposals.rationale: R43 sounds like an interrupted Southern conversational setup, and R54 performs a familiar reckless boast.

proposals.name: Novel lexical collision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when uncommon words are combined into a surprising but immediately coherent comic image; score 0 when the phrase is a familiar cliché or routine pairing.
proposals.rationale: R01 pairs blandness with outer space, and R59 collides NASCAR with the dating phrase chill.

proposals.name: Reference-independent humor
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke remains understandable without recognizing the named film, celebrity, or franchise; score 0 when recognition is nearly the entire mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R12, R22, and R27 depend heavily on familiarity with Star Wars rather than supplying a self-contained comic situation.

proposals.name: Depth beyond title substitution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a borrowed title structure is transformed into a specific new situation through several interacting changes; score 0 when it is mostly a single obvious word replacement.
proposals.rationale: R34 and R55 largely substitute a political term into a familiar title, offering limited development beyond the template.

proposals.name: Reference-stacking clutter
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when multiple names or borrowed references crowd out a single coherent premise; score 0 when every reference is necessary and mutually reinforces one joke.
proposals.rationale: R49 and R56 accumulate several recognizable names, making the intended comic target less focused.

proposals.name: Shock reliance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when taboo, sexual, or gross material supplies nearly all of the effect without an additional comic mechanism; score 0 when any shock element is subordinate to strong wordplay or narrative.
proposals.rationale: R15 and R21 rely primarily on incestuous sexual shock, while R40 relies primarily on grotesque anatomy.

proposals.name: Stereotype-list dependence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when familiar identity markers are merely accumulated to signal a type; score 0 when each element creates a distinct premise, contrast, or turn.
proposals.rationale: R03 strings together stereotyped redneck objects, and R07 similarly assembles possum and casserole markers without a strong transformation.

proposals.name: Prompt-generic phrasing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording could be reused under many unrelated prompts with little change; score 0 when it is uniquely tailored to this exact prompt.
proposals.rationale: R31 is a broadly reusable advertising slogan, and R33 is a generic food description rather than a tightly tailored premise.

proposals.name: Contest-wrapper regularity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the tweet uses a repeated, formulaic placement and spacing of the contest hashtag and @midnight; judge only wrapper regularity, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: Posting tools or venue conventions can create stable textual signatures that a text model learns as reception proxies without measuring contest quality. Compare R01, R04, R18, and R53.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission mechanism and participation workflow

proposals.name: Late-riff textual stance
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the wording reads as a late-arriving riff that assumes obvious interpretations or familiar references are already circulating; judge only this textual stance, not whether the riff is good.
proposals.rationale: Crowding and submission order may leave traces such as sequel references or riffs on already familiar premises, which can affect reception independently of quality; later-positioned work can also genuinely differ in quality. Compare R19, R20, R54, and R60.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream and submission timing

proposals.name: Named-entity density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the amount of explicit naming of people, places, brands, franchises, institutions, or public figures; judge only the quantity and salience of names, not whether using them is good.
proposals.rationale: References can exploit audience recognition or author-audience overlap, creating a reception shortcut unrelated to intrinsic quality, although reference choice can also genuinely matter. Compare R10, R19, R31, and R37.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience familiarity and following

proposals.name: Taboo-content density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of sexual, incestuous, bodily, or otherwise taboo vocabulary; judge only how much taboo material is present, not whether it is funny, effective, or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Taboo vocabulary may trigger attention, filtering, or learned stylistic associations without constituting contest quality. Compare R08, R13, R24, R47, and R58.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Political identity cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit partisan, ideological, governmental, electoral, or political-identity language; judge only the presence of those cues, not whether the political reference is good.
proposals.rationale: Political identity cues can activate audience alignment and visibility effects that are not quality measures, while political topicality can sometimes genuinely contribute to an entry. Compare R01, R03, R04, R31, and R43.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience or following alignment with polarized topics

proposals.name: Stock-template wording
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text resembles a familiar slogan, quotation, title, catchphrase, or pre-existing verbal template; judge only template resemblance, not whether the reuse is good.
proposals.rationale: Reusable phrases can benefit from audience recognition and author familiarity with the format, producing a predictive shortcut distinct from intrinsic quality; template adaptation can also genuinely matter. Compare R17, R39, R53, R55, R57, and R59.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's reliance on familiar cultural templates and format practice

proposals.name: Orthographic irregularity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of misspellings, grammatical anomalies, malformed wording, or unusual encoding artifacts; judge only visible irregularity, not whether the text is good.
proposals.rationale: Hasty entry or editing workflow can leave visible errors that correlate with how text is received without directly measuring quality, though such errors can sometimes affect genuine clarity. Compare R12, R28, R33, and R38.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission haste, mobile entry, or external editing

proposals.name: Emphatic typography
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the amount of all-caps wording, repeated punctuation, theatrical capitalization, or other typographic emphasis; judge only the intensity of the formatting, not whether it improves the entry.
proposals.rationale: Emphatic formatting can attract attention or resemble a venue-specific style, creating a text-model shortcut unrelated to contest quality. Compare R07, R42, R49, and R50.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Telegraphic list syntax
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the tweet consists of fragments, compressed noun groups, or comma-separated lists rather than a conventional clause; judge only syntactic form, not whether the form is good.
proposals.rationale: Format-practiced authors may use a recognizable compressed syntax that predicts reception independently of quality, although control of that syntax can also genuinely affect quality. Compare R25, R40, R51, and R52.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the one-line contest format

proposals.name: Markup or link residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of visible URLs, HTML entities, or other copy-paste and markup residue; judge only the residue's presence, not whether it is useful or harmful.
proposals.rationale: Posting or editing pipelines can leave machine-readable artifacts that a text model associates with distribution or reception while measuring no intrinsic contest quality. Compare R10 and R33.
proposals.upstream_parent: copy-paste or external editing assistance
